messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina was 23 and worked as a ship captain, a job that had once felt like proof that she could keep herself moving forward and in control. In the intake interviews she spoke quietly, with the kind of precision that suggested she had learned early to measure danger before it arrived. Her childhood memories centered on a father who could turn physically abusive without warning, striking her in the darkened hallway or in rooms where she could not immediately see where he stood. She remembered waking at night with her body already braced, listening for footsteps, and being punished for not reacting quickly enough. Now, years later, the old fear had not stayed in the past. It returned most sharply at night, when she woke in the dark and for a moment could not tell where she was, and when she had to drive with other people in the car, especially if a man was sitting beside her or behind her. In those moments her body became rigid and ready, her shoulders locked high, her stomach hollow, as if she had to prepare instantly for impact. She described herself as constantly tense and on alert, and said that the feeling was not just discomfort but a physical certainty that something bad could happen at any second.

Mina had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that belief made each of those situations feel loaded before they even began. If she had to park the truck at the dock after dark, or wake in her apartment to a black room, she would scan the shadows and check doors twice, convinced that people—especially men—could appear anywhere and hurt her before she could think. She was also haunted by the sense that there was something wrong with her, that other people moved through life with a basic ease she did not have because she had been marked by what happened to her. That feeling of being defective fed a deeper isolation; she kept most relationships superficial, told herself it was safer not to explain, and noticed how separate she felt from coworkers who joked casually in the galley or accepted a ride home without hesitation. When her mind settled on the idea that she was unlike other people in some damaged way, she became even more wary of being alone with men or trapped in a vehicle with someone else, as if her own difference made her more exposed.

The same fear that kept her vigilant also seemed to summon the very situations she dreaded. Once she had been tense all afternoon before a night shift because her supervisor asked her to give a male deckhand a ride back to the marina office, and by the time he climbed into the passenger seat she was already searching for exits, rehearsing what she would do if he reached for her or if the route changed. She knew the plan of every road leading away from the docks, and before she could feel comfortable anywhere she automatically identified escape routes, checking where she could pull over, where she could run, which doors would open fastest. At night this became even worse: waking in the dark sent her mind immediately to danger, and because she saw the world as dangerous and herself as somehow vulnerable in a special, personal way, she was more likely to notice the things that fit that fear—a man lingering outside the fuel station, a car slowing near her, a dark stairwell—and to treat them as proof that her caution was necessary. The more she expected threat, the more every dark room, every ride with others, every isolated encounter with a man seemed to confirm it.

The strain showed in her body long before she admitted she needed help. Her muscles stayed tight through long watches at sea, and she said she could never quite settle, even when the ship was calm. If the engine room went quiet after midnight, she would feel her whole system sharpen, ready to react to danger before she had any evidence of it. That watchfulness narrowed her life. She avoided unnecessary drives with colleagues, declined invitations that would leave her alone with male friends, and began sleeping badly enough that she was irritable and distant on board. It was humiliating to her that a young woman who could navigate tides and equipment could not relax in a dark corridor or accept a ride without scanning every possibility of escape. She had grown increasingly withdrawn, telling herself that isolation was safer than being caught off guard, but the isolation only made the world seem larger and more dangerous.

By the time she sought therapy, Mina was exhausted by how much of her day was organized around anticipating harm. A recent night in port had become the tipping point: she woke in the dark cabin of her own apartment, heart already pounding, and later that week found herself frozen when a male coworker offered her a lift after a late shift. She came in because she was afraid the constant tension was becoming her whole life, and because she did not want to keep living as if every night, every car, and every man might be the place where the past returned. What she hoped for, though she said it almost apologetically, was to feel less broken and to believe that she could move through the world without always looking for the nearest way out.
